articles.body:
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.

The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.

Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.

“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.

The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.

A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.

Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.

“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.

Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.

Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.

Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.

She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.

According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.

More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.

The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.

According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

articles.title: UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military
articles.summary: UK authorities have passed the investigation to the US 'in line with existing international protocols'.
articles.preview: United Kingdom authorities have passed the investigation to the United States ‘in line with existing international protocols’. A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said. The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.
articles.body:
United Kingdom authorities have passed the investigation to the United States ‘in line with existing international protocols’.

A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said.

The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”.

The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.

Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.

He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”

US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.

Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.

The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

articles.title: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
articles.summary: Russia's defence ministry says it preliminarily believes a technical malfunction was the cause of the crash in the Kemerovo region.
articles.preview: A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media. The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement. The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
articles.body:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.

The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.

Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".

The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.

He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.

The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.

An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

articles.title: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody
articles.summary: Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said. articles.body:
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.

Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating to espionage.

The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.

The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.

“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.

“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command. Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”

The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.

He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.

US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.

He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.

As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.

“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.

“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.

“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.

US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution.”

He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.

“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

articles.title: Trump in Asia ahead of talks with Russian and Chinese presidents
articles.summary: The US president said he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin "if it's available".
articles.preview: US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin. A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.

A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.

Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with US partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese.

"Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said.

"We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.

Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.

The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.

But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.

Later on Tuesday, Trump signed a trade deal with Thailand alongside the country's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year.

Trump then joined South East Asia leaders at a dinner, telling those gathered: "This is one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions filled with the tremendous potential."

After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".

articles.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.summary: It marks the first sanctions since the UK announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
articles.preview: The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory. The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank. The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years.
articles.body:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.

The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".

"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".

Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.

"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.

"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

'New approach'

In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".

That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel, which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.

Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.body:
Come è nato il buddismo? Come si è trasformato nei secoli? E in che modo si è adattato alle diverse condizioni sociali e storiche dei paesi in cui si è affermato? In Lungo le strade del Budda lo scrittore britannico di origine indiana e pachistana Aatish Taseer racconta lo sviluppo della tradizione filosofica e religiosa che ha cambiato il volto dell’Asia seguendo le tracce della sua diffusione e delle sue mutazioni.

Il libro è una raccolta di tre reportage: un viaggio che comincia nel luogo di nascita del Budda, in Nepal, prosegue in Thailandia, dove la dottrina si è alleata con la politica, e si conclude a Taiwan, l’isola che custodisce ancora l’eredità spirituale e culturale della vecchia Cina.

Lungo le strade del Budda è l’ottavo libro di Extra Large, la collana dei tascabili di Internazionale, pensata per far conoscere a lettrici e lettori reportage, inchieste, articoli e racconti di grande qualità narrativa e giornalistica ma troppo lunghi per essere pubblicati sul settimanale. Il progetto grafico è di Mark Porter.

Lungo le strade del Budda è un volume di 96 pagine, in formato tascabile, in vendita a 7 euro in tutte le edicole, nelle principali librerie online (tra cui Ibs, La Feltrinelli, Hoepli, Amazon), e a 3,99 euro in formato ebook, anche per Kindle e per Kobo.

articles.title: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
articles.summary: The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.
articles.preview: November 17, 2026 The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan. During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.
articles.body:
November 17, 2026

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

What does Russia mean by 1997?

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

Who decides which alliances a country can join?

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Why is the demand back on the table?

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

articles.body:
Cada año desde 2010, el departamento de Medio Ambiente de Naciones Unidas, conocido por las siglas Pnuma, analiza la distancia que existe entre los planes nacionales de recorte de emisiones de efecto invernadero y los objetivos climáticos que se autoimponen los países en los tratados internacionales. En el Acuerdo de París , de 2015, el tratado de referencia ahora, se estableció que las emisiones mundiales debían caer a una velocidad e intensidad suficientes para que el calentamiento no superara los 2 grados Celsius y, en la medida de lo posible, los 1,5, respecto a los niveles preindustriales.

El aumento de la temperatura global se ha ido acercando al galope hacia la primera barrera, pero el Pnuma seguía manteniendo abierta una ventana para poder cumplir con París. Hasta este año, cuando admitió la dura realidad : el primer dique de contención se romperá a finales de esta década o principios de la siguiente, y el calentamiento va a superar los 1,5 grados. articles.title: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
articles.summary: Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
articles.preview: November 17, 2026 Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain? The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week. Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
articles.body:
November 17, 2026

Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?

The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.

Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.

Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.

Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."

Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.

"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.

"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."

Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.

Contentious issues may be left for later

Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.

She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.

Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."

She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.

With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.

China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas

Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.

Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.

"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."

Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.

"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."

Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.

An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."

The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.

He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."

He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.

"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.

"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."

Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation

W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.

The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."

Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.

"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

BEIJING: China condemned on Tuesday (Nov 17) new United States curbs on chip exports and vowed to take "necessary measures" after Washington moved to close a loophole under intense scrutiny following the Nvidia spy scandal.
articles.body:
Washington announced new restrictions on AI chip exports which will require data centres anywhere in the world to have a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China and several other countries.

BEIJING: China condemned on Tuesday (Nov 17) new United States curbs on chip exports and vowed to take "necessary measures" after Washington moved to close a loophole under intense scrutiny following the Nvidia spy scandal.

Washington announced new restrictions on Monday on AI chip exports which will require data centres anywhere in the world to have a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil - countries the US commerce department says present a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips.

Beijing's foreign ministry denounced the curbs on Tuesday.

"The US repeatedly overstretches the concept of national security, abusing export control measures," ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing, vowing that China will "take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests".

The country's commerce ministry also expressed "firm opposition" to the new restrictions, urging the US to "return to the right track of resolving differences" through consultation and cooperation.

"Such actions ... undermine market rules and the international economic and trade order, and threaten the stability of global semiconductor industrial and supply chains," the ministry said in a statement late Tuesday, also threatening Washington with countermeasures.

articles.title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine says the missile and drone attack on the strategic bridge in the Russian-annexed Crimea took weeks to plan.
articles.preview: Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort. The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
articles.body:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.

The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.

The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.

In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.

"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.

He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".

Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."

The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".

The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.

Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.

The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.

On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title: Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
articles.summary: Whistleblower accuses military of dismissing advanced security warnings of drone strike that killed six US soldiers.
articles.preview: Whistleblower accuses the military of dismissing advanced security warnings of a drone strike that killed six US soldiers in Kuwait. Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.
articles.body:
Whistleblower accuses the military of dismissing advanced security warnings of a drone strike that killed six US soldiers in Kuwait.

Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.

The complaint, obtained by Al Jazeera English on Tuesday, is tied to an Iranian one-way attack drone that evaded air defences at the outpost within the first 48 hours of the war. Six service members were killed, and dozens were injured, including the whistleblower. It remains the deadliest assault on US forces since the war commenced.

The 14-page letter, submitted on Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, alleges that the army repeatedly brushed aside warnings that the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait was vulnerable to drone attacks. Though the site was fortified, there was no roof.

“The drone threat to the port was raised directly to the commanding general of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command at least three times in the week before hostilities,” the complaint states.

“Each warning was dismissed.”

The soldier, who is not named, also alleges the installation had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance”, adding that at least one of those killed “could have survived” if there was adequate medical support on site.

The army says it has completed its investigation of the Port of Shuaiba attack but has not publicly released its findings.

In a news conference following the incident, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the drone as a “squirter” that “happened to hit a tactical operations centre that was fortified”.

But senior military leaders have acknowledged that Iran’s Shahed attack drones, known to fly low and slow, have inflicted more damage on the battlefield than anticipated.

Tehran has repeatedly targeted US and allied assets with attack drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, more than 23 American service members have been killed.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the allegations.

articles.title: US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces
articles.summary: Lawmakers hound Hung Cao over expanding war, opaque leadership shake-ups, and low crew morale at confirmation hearing.
articles.preview: Lawmakers press Hung Cao over expanding war, opaque leadership shake-ups, and low crew morale in confirmation hearing. United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has acknowledged that the Iran war is taxing the maritime service as bipartisan senators questioned him over extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and resources being shifted away from the Asia-Pacific.
articles.body:
Lawmakers press Hung Cao over expanding war, opaque leadership shake-ups, and low crew morale in confirmation hearing.

United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has acknowledged that the Iran war is taxing the maritime service as bipartisan senators questioned him over extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and resources being shifted away from the Asia-Pacific.

Testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday at his confirmation hearing to lead the military branch, Cao faced sharp, bipartisan grilling over the mounting human and material costs of the US-Israel war on Iran, which is now deep into its ninth month.

“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” Cao said, while insisting that joint military efforts have “really set China back on their heels”.

Cao, a retired US Navy captain and former Republican Party candidate for the Virginia Senate, has served as acting navy secretary since April 2026 after previously holding the under-secretary post.

The candidate, backed by US President Donald Trump, is now seeking US Senate confirmation for the permanent top civilian job.

The hearing comes amid burgeoning political fallout over the protracted quagmire with Iran, which recently saw a failed US House bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his stewardship of the war.

Voter frustration over the war — and its economic sting — proved decisive in the November midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and ultimately cost the Republicans control of both the House and the Senate.

The Democratic-controlled 120th Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

Heated Senate exchange

As the ranking Democrat on the committee, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island questioned Cao during the nearly two-hour hearing, saying he was candidly troubled by his performance so far.

“I am concerned, frankly, about your leadership record as acting secretary,” said Reed, who called on the acting US Navy secretary to speak to Hegseth‘s ongoing and planned dismissals of numerous naval officers over the past year, pressing Cao on whether he would “defend the military leaders in the future from partisan meddling in their careers”.

Democratic lawmakers went on to criticise the US Navy for bypassing standard congressional notification after quietly relieving the entire leadership team — the commander, executive officer and command master chief — of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota following an October underwater collision with the seabed.

“We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternisation or, you know, harassment,” Cao said, making the case against the US Navy’s traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders. “I want to make sure that we’re protecting their livelihood afterwards as well.”

His stated intent to safeguard individuals’ careers was promptly rebuked by Reed, who maintained that privacy does not justify shielding information from congressional oversight.

“The squadron commodore [of the USS South Dakota] felt that they did not live up to their honour, courage, and commitment ethos, and therefore, he relieved the commanding officer, the executive officer, and the command master chief,” Cao countered.

Cao’s record on sailor mental health comes under fire

The US Navy chief-nominee also faced intense questioning from lawmakers about low crew morale, severe supply shortages, and mental health strains aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln following its record-breaking 265-day deployment in the Pacific Ocean, South China Sea, Indian Ocean, and North Arabian Sea.

The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, in early October after the USS George Washington arrived on station to relieve it. Together with the USS George HW Bush and the newly arrived USS Theodore Roosevelt, the US is temporarily massing three carrier strike groups to bolster regional maritime security and tighten the months-long naval blockade against Iran.

Last week, Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. He noted, however, that the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, argued that Cao was “failing these sailors and their families”, and noted that his “confrontation with them leaves me with the clear impression that you simply don’t care”.

Cao pushed back, declaring that he does not control the deployment lengths of US Navy ships that have crept steadily closer to a full year at sea — up from a standard of six to eight months during the US’s so-called “war on terror”.

“Sustained investment in our people will increase readiness, improve retention and recruitment, and enable our ability to support national objectives,” said Cao.

When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Blumenthal that what he saw “as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations”.

Cao faces a rare waiver hurdle for the top spot

In his opening statement, Republican Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker expressed support for Cao’s nomination to lead the US Navy, noting that while the service faces significant challenges during a particularly volatile time, it also has major opportunities.

Beyond fielding tough questions from lawmakers on Tuesday over the strain of the Iran war on fleet readiness, Cao still faces a complex confirmation path to become the permanent secretary of the navy, requiring a rare congressional waiver.

Because he left active-duty service in October 2021, he falls short of the seven-year separation period mandated by federal law to preserve civilian control of the military.

Securing that exemption poses a steep political climb for Cao, who must clear the hurdle by meeting a 60-vote threshold, which may prove tricky in a polarised Washington.

Cao will ultimately need cross-party support from Democrats or independents to avoid a filibuster, while winning over war-sceptical Republicans.

articles.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
articles.summary: Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.
articles.preview: Kosovo: New Thaci conviction reignites debate about justice November 17, 2026 Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him. A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
articles.body:
Kosovo: New Thaci conviction reignites debate about justice

November 17, 2026

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

Parliament considers amending law

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

Un clamoroso schiaffo nella guerra dei ponti colpisce lo zar del Cremlino, Vladimir Putin, in vista dell'atteso trilaterale cinese con Xi Jinping e Donald Trump: gli ucraini sono infatti riusciti a distruggere il ponte di Kerch, che collega la Russia con la Crimea. Anzi collegava, perché ora il traffico è sostanzialmente interrotto dopo i missili che hanno centrato la struttura.

Mosca minimizza: "Lo ricostruiremo". Mentre Kiev esulta ma è costretta a fare i conti a sua volta con i nuovi raid russi che hanno preso di mira la capitale ucraina: il traffico sui ponti Pivnichnyi (nord) e Pivdennyi (sud) è stato nuovamente sospeso, creando immensi disagi, mentre altri raid hanno causato interruzioni al sistema idrico e di riscaldamento. Danneggiati anche alcuni tratti dei binari di superfice della metropolitana.

"La Russia colpisce quotidianamente le nostre infrastrutture, compresi i ponti, a Zaporizhia, Dnipro, Kiev e nella regione di Odessa, quella in Crimea è una operazione senza precedenti condotta in risposta a questi attacchi", ha sottolineato il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky, pubblicando la sequenza di un missile Flamingo 'made in Kiev' che colpisce il ponte Kerch. L'azienda che lo produce ha celebrato l'attacco con un emoticon stile pop corn.

I danni al ponte di Crimea, fiore all'occhiello dello zar che lo inaugurò nel 2018 attraversandolo alla guida di un camion Kamaz, sembrano molto consistenti: missili e droni hanno fatto collassare una campata di 227 metri dell'arco stradale, con i resti dell'arco di sostegno e dell'impalcato che sporgono dall'acqua sottostante. Anche la campata adiacente dell'arco ferroviario ha subito danni, ma il tratto parallelo a quello crollato sembra intatto. I detriti però sembrano ostruire del tutto il tratto navigabile sotto il ponte, che collega il Mar d'Azov al Mar Nero: il canale è largo 120 metri e profondo poco più di 8, i pezzi in acciaio sommersi potrebbero impedire il passaggio di imbarcazioni di grandi dimensioni fino a quando i detriti non saranno rimossi. Il blocco complica ancora di più l'approvvigionamento, non solo militare, della Crimea, già reso difficile da altri attacchi al ponte, nel 2022 con un camion imbottito di esplosivo l'anno successivo con i droni marini, e dalle minacce consistenti per le altre due rotte di rifornimento dalla Russia, lungo la linea del fronte orientale, e l'altra via mare.

Video

Da Bruxelles fanno sapere che la struttura "costituisce una via di rifornimento per le truppe di Mosca e riveste un enorme valore simbolico, Kiev ha tutto il diritto di colpirlo". Al gruppo di contatto per la difesa dell'Ucraina, Zelensky ha quindi lanciato l'idea di uno scambio: "Abbiamo bisogno ora di intercettori Patriot e Iris-T dalle scorte che già avete e in cambio possiamo darvi i nuovi missili che l'Ucraina ha già ordinato, quando saranno prodotti". "Voi ci date i missili di cui abbiamo bisogno adesso e in cambio ricevete missili più nuovi e migliori", ha spiegato, chiedendo agli Stati Uniti di "non ritardare" le consegne.

Ma dalla stessa riunione nella capitale Ue è arrivato anche il monito del sottosegretario alla Difesa americano Elbridge Colby: "Mentre il dibattito pubblico si concentra sullo spettacolo degli attacchi in profondità pensati per infliggere dolore alla popolazione russa, la nostra valutazione è che non siano stati efficaci nel portare alla fine della guerra, né contribuiscano a frenare l'avanzata russa al fronte". Inoltre, con l'arrivo dell'inverno, l'Ucraina avrà bisogno di "finanziamenti solidi, questa responsabilità ricadrà però soprattutto sulle spalle dell'Europa".

Un intervento che sembra destinato a scatenare una scia di polemiche, mentre sul fronte diplomatico Parigi getta acqua sul fuoco: sostenere che i soldati francesi presenti in Ucraina partecipino direttamente al conflitto, come dichiarato dal ministro degli Esteri russo Serghei Lavrov, è "assurdo", ha detto la ministra francese con delega alle Forze armate, Alice Rufo, sottolineando che si tratta di militari impegnati esclusivamente in missioni di addestramento e manutenzione.

Parole che non hanno convinto Lavrov: "Credo che il personale militare straniero sia presente in Ucraina da più di sei mesi. E non si tratta solo di personale francese". Mosca ha "avvertito i Paesi interessati che non si tratta più di un sostegno all'Ucraina, ma di una partecipazione diretta alla guerra".

articles.title: Israel's genocide in Gaza continues. So must the protests
articles.summary: Israel's genocide in Gaza continues. So must the protests Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 16:27 Demonstrations gave Palestinians hope and pressured institutions to act. A ceasefire that has failed to stop the killing must not become a reason for silence Demonstrators at the Red Line march in Amsterdam, Netherlands, on 8 November 2026, demand that the Dutch government take stronger action against Israel over its genocide in Gaza (Mouafak Mahmalji/Zuma Press Wire via Reuters) Off At 9pm every night during the first weeks of Israel's genocide in Gaza , around 30 people and their children in the home where I was displaced would gather in an empty space in front of the house. Many of them wrapped themselves in woollen blankets, some sitting on the ground, others standing, looking for their daily "dose of hope" on a television screen. With no electricity, we used the little power the available solar panels could collect from the sun all day to turn on the TV and watch the news for around 30 minutes. Once the familiar news theme played, those gathering around the screen started calling on others inside the house to hurry and join them. Among them, I stood, very well aware that those sparkling eyes would not find what they were looking for. They would find no international action taken against the war crimes , crimes against humanity and genocide we were witnessing, no appropriate international condemnation, and not even a statement by a world leader clearly naming the perpetrators. Sitting on a concrete bench with an old displaced man from the shelter next to ours who came to watch the news with us, I whispered: "Do you still hope to see meaningful international action taken this time?" He told me he was not watching the news in anticipation of any action by world governments, but found solace in seeing updates about the protests sweeping the streets of countries around the world. As a Palestinian trying to survive the next hour, and like the around two million Palestinians trapped in this sealed space and feeling like they were being hunted, one after another, his answer made sense to me. Watching people outside this space taking to the streets indeed made victims of the ongoing genocide feel less abandoned. Perhaps this was all they were looking for at the time, being well aware that, for more than 75 years of military occupation and 17 years of a strangling blockade , the international community had proven incapable of stopping Israel's war crimes. More than comfort Gradually, over the following months, the protests provided much more than mere comfort to Palestinians in Gaza. At some point, protesters around the world managed to turn solidarity from mere slogans into real organised pressure on institutions capable of taking tangible steps and making concrete decisions, at a time when world leaders lacked the political will to act. Demonstrators across Europe and other western countries demanded that their governments stop funding and supplying arms to Israel, and called on universities and other institutions to divest and reconsider their partnerships with entities directly or indirectly linked to human rights violations in the occupied Palestinian territory. Some of those protests resulted in real, tangible steps by several institutions. Sustained solidarity could move institutions from expressions of concern to decisions affecting their investments and partnerships At Trinity College Dublin , for example, a student encampment pressured the university to agree to divest from Israeli companies listed by the United Nations for their activities in the occupied Palestinian territory, making it one of the first universities to do so. Later, the university confirmed it had divested and approved wider divestment . In Belgium, after weeks of protests on the campus of Ghent University , the university yielded to protesters' demands and decided to sever ties and end collaborations with "certain Israeli governmental and academic institutions", and further urged the European Commission to exclude Israeli partners from European-funded programmes and projects. While these achievements did not put an end to the massacres at the time and were relatively limited compared with the scale of Palestinian suffering and the urgent need to hold the perpetrators accountable, they still restored some hope to a people long failed by international promises. They demonstrated, first-hand, that sustained solidarity could move institutions from expressions of concern to decisions affecting their investments and partnerships. From Gaza, this mattered. The people filling those streets were practically challenging decisions made and relations maintained with the perpetrators in countries whose policies could help determine whether those of us still alive would survive. After the ceasefire A few months after the ceasefire agreement took effect on 10 October 2025, Palestinians in Gaza started reclaiming glimpses of normal life, repairing basic telecommunications infrastructure alongside other essential infrastructure. Being connected to the outside world has always been a means of breathing for a people who have long defied attempts at isolation. As neighbourhoods across the devastated strip gradually began restoring internet connections, Palestinians consistently followed the news on their phones, hoping to see real action on the ground, especially as the attacks, displacement and killings persisted. For more than a year following the ceasefire agreement, Israel has continued the genocide at a slower pace that is intense enough to keep seizing land, displacing Palestinians and claiming lives every single day, yet quiet enough to allow international condemnation and outrage to subside. Gaza flooding is a catastrophe by design - and the spineless West is complicit ent and a US plan for Gaza's future drawn up without the involvement of Palestinians in Gaza, a second phase of the genocide began, with less international attention , very limited media coverage and, eventually, far fewer protests, many of them silenced by government repression and university crackdowns . Meeting with Palestinians on the ground, I have heard many say that this sense of abandonment has been one of the most devastating consequences of this phase, compounding the pain of surviving the genocide. For the first time since the outset of the genocide, Palestinians in Gaza now feel abandoned not only by world governments, whose inaction they have endured for decades, but also by the people around the world who once gave them strength and hope simply by taking to the streets, raising their voices and demanding accountability for the perpetrators. As Palestinians in Gaza struggle to stay alive and plead with the world to keep speaking out, it is more urgent than ever to understand that when the loudspeakers at protests fall quiet, the bombs on Gaza grow louder and heavier with a sense of abandonment that has long allowed such crimes to continue.
