articles.body:
At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”

The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.body:
Saudi Arabia: Crackdown on dissent intensifies amid Iran war

November 17, 2026

Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Leah Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

articles.body:
Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.

The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.

Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.

That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.

Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.

Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.

It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.

Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.

Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.

Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.

If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.

Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.

A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.

The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.

Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.

“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

Zelenskyy urges partners to send air defence deliveries without delay as Russia intensifies attacks

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he addressed ministers during the Ukraine Defence Support Group in Brussels.

“Russia keeps attacking us with jet-powered Shaheed drones, cruise missiles, and, most dangerously, ballistic missiles, and we need to defend against all of this,” he said.

“The world has enough [of air defence missiles] and America has them, some European countries have them, and some of our other partners around the world have them, too. These interceptors should not be sitting in warehouses. They should be in air defence batteries, protecting our cities, towns and villages from Russian strikes and saving lives, of course.”

“We all understand that there are long waiting lists for new interceptors, but we need them here and now,” he added.

Zelenskyy warned that “every successful Russian strike makes Russia more aggressive, more demanding, and less willing to compromise.”

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he dialled into a meeting of Ukraine’s key allies at a high-level meeting in Brussels (17:07).

The renewed request came hours after Ukraine critically damaged the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, in what Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation which drew comments from allies (10:32, 14:55, 15:01, 17:34).

Several European partners, including Denmark, Germany, Sweden and the UK, declared their plans to further support Ukraine amid growing concerns about a particularly difficult winter ahead (9:55, 9:58, 16:01, 17:11).

On Thursday, top EU leaders are going to meet in Berlin for latest talks on Ukraine within the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb saying the meeting will be “very important” to help influence the structure of any peace talks with Russia (13:03).

In other news,

46 people were injured, including four seriously, after two commuter trains collided near the main railway station in Prague (10:09).

Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, have been sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government. (13:46).

Former US president Joe Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, got published today, with some of his unfiltered views on Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, Ukraine, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Brexit (13:41).

After 65 days without a government, the Swedish outgoing prime minister and Moderates leader Ulf Kristersson has asked for more time before parliament votes on whether they want him as prime minister (15:50, 16:29).

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Collapsed part of the Kerch Bridge was once described as technically most challenging part of structure - snap analysis

Pjotr Sauer

The section of the Crimean Bridge that appears to have collapsed in Tuesday’s attack was described by Russian engineers at the time of its construction as the most technically challenging part of the entire project.

Dmitry Kondakov, a senior executive at the company building the bridge, said in 2016 that shipping arches were “the most difficult thing we have to do”, noting that Russia had little experience constructing such complex structures.

Another senior official described the operation to install the arches as the “pinnacle of the entire construction project”, calling it the most technically demanding stage of building the bridge.

Their comments highlight the complexity of the rebuild operation planned by Russia (11:12).

The US undersecretary of defence Elbridge Colby has praised Europe for stepping up to take more responsibility for Ukraine’s defence, helping mount the Ukrainian forces mount “a resilient denial defence.”

Colby said Europe and the US “have made tremendous progress in making Nato 3.0 a reality,” while continuing to support Ukraine.

But he said more needs to be done, urging Europe “to focus its defence industrial-based efforts on military efficacy and battlefield utility, rather than ancillary domestic or industrial policy objectives” and continue its spending on Ukraine-related schemes.

Turning to Ukraine, he said:

“In October, for the second consecutive month, Ukraine gained more territory than Russia and Russian forces suffered their highest monthly casualty toll of the war.”

But in a rather curious part of his statement, Colby appeared to distance the US from some of the recent deep strikesin Russia.

He argued:

“It is our view that focusing on support, our support on the frontlines and on associated mid-range strikes is the most effective way to enable Ukraine’s defence, and thus to set the conditions for an end to the war. …

While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the frontline.

Moreover, such strikes as especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate. Moreover, it is important to note that the balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favour Moscow.”

He added:

“This is not to say that Ukraine should be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back. Rather, that we should be clear about is that the focus of our support should be on enabling and advancing Ukraine’s ability to hold the line of battle and, where possible, make gains.

Strikes focused on the frontline and direct support to that battle area, of course, fall into this category, but consistent with this approach, strikes that target Russia’s war making machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advances on the frontlines.”

Colby also said the US administration “remain firmly committed to bringing this conflict to an end on terms that secure a durable peace,” even as it appears that Russia wants to continue the war.

Russia could 'try to cause humanitarian emergencies' in large cities to break Ukraine's resolve, German minister warns

Germany’s defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that “the fifth war winter … threatens to be harder than the ones before,” as Russia “has further expanded its arsenal of attack drones and ballistic missiles.”

“With daily airstrikes, Russia is trying to take out Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and water supply. It is terrorising Ukraine from the air because it cannot achieve military success on the ground,” he said.

Pistorius warned that Russia “may intentionally try to cause humanitarian emergencies in Kyiv, Odesa and other large cities to break the Ukrainian people’s resistance.”

“If Russia were to succeed, the consequence would be dramatic, both for Ukraine and for Europe,” he said.

Earlier, UK’s Wes Streeting said the aim of the meeting is to discuss how to “put Ukraine in the best possible position for future negotiations.”

Zelenskyy urges partners to send air defence deliveries without delay as Russia intensifies attacks

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he addressed ministers during the Ukraine Defence Support Group in Brussels.

“Russia keeps attacking us with jet-powered Shaheed drones, cruise missiles, and, most dangerously, ballistic missiles, and we need to defend against all of this,” he said.

“The world has enough [of air defence missiles] and America has them, some European countries have them, and some of our other partners around the world have them, too. These interceptors should not be sitting in warehouses. They should be in air defence batteries, protecting our cities, towns and villages from Russian strikes and saving lives, of course.”

“We all understand that there are long waiting lists for new interceptors, but we need them here and now,” he added.

Zelenskyy warned that “every successful Russian strike makes Russia more aggressive, more demanding, and less willing to compromise.”

Swedish parliament speaker wants to see new government or snap poll called by Christmas

Miranda Bryant

Nordic correspondent

The Speaker of the Riksdag, Andreas Norlén, has said granted Ulf Kristersson’s request for more time for coalition talks (15:50) but that he wants to have clarity for the Swedish public by Christmas.

He said he would give parties one more week before he calls in the party leaders to decide what will happen next, but that he is determined to get to the end of this process soon so that by Christmas, Sweden will either have a new government or can prepare to go back to the polls with a second election.

He said:

“My opinion is that this formation of government needs to come to an end in good time before Christmas. I want that when the Swedish people celebrate Christmas they will know that Sweden either has a new government or are preparing themselves for another election.”

Swedish minister says he has 'not seen any serious intent' from Russia to negotiate Ukraine peace

Sticking to the Swedish theme for a moment, Sweden’s defence minister Pål Jonson is the latest leader to stop by the journalists upon his arrival at today’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels.

In his comments, he said the meeting was “timely” as “the situation in Ukraine is very challenging due to the fact that Russia scaled up its production, both of ballistic missiles and also drones and glide bombs.”

Sweden will spend €4bn on helping Ukraine in 2027, Jonson said, noting cross-party backing across the parliament.

The minister also said that Sweden signed a letter of intent with Ukraine and the UK on the upcoming delivery of Gripen fighter jets for Ukraine.

Responding to questions from reporters, Jonson also said that the US undersecretary of defence Colby did not say “specific” information on the ongoing review of the US posture in Europe.

“We are expecting it to come by the end of the year,” he said, adding that “the message is clear that Europe is going to shouldering the lion’s share of conventional deterrence by 2028.”

Asked about the peace negotiations with Russia, the Swedish minister said he “has not seen any serious intent from the Russian side” on ending the war in Ukraine, stressing the need to keep supporting Kyiv in the meantime.

Jonson pointedly disagreed with Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, who has repeatedly called for direct talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

Asked if he sees any merit in that approach, he said:“Not quite, because we do not see any serious commitment from the Russian side to making any kind of compromise.”

“I know there’s all kinds of ideas drifting around that we should also have a discussion about the European security architecture. We do not welcome that.”

Sweden's Kristersson asks parliament speaker for more time to form new government

Miranda Bryant

Nordic correspondent

In other news, after 65 days without a government, Moderates leader Ulf Kristersson has asked for more time before parliament votes on whether they want him as prime minister.

Two weeks after he was given the task to attempt to form a “middle” coalition government by the Speaker, he said on Tuesday afternoon that he had requested a few more days.

The Speaker will hold a press conference later this afternoon when he is expected to respond to the former prime minister’s request.

His announcement comes after the Centre party leader, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, asked Kristersson and the Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson to present a “total package” for her party to choose between after talks between the left-leaning parties failed to produce a result.

She has already said yes to Andersson’s proposal of a coalition between the Social Democrats, Green party and the Centre party with cooperation with the Left party. But the Left party has since continued to demand ministerial posts, which the Centre party has refused to accept.

Kristersson said:

“A majority government that cannot agree does not work, so nothing would get done. A few more days are needed before a vote takes place, so that the Centre party can have a complete basis for decision making which is needed to take a position.”

If the vote on Kristersson does not lead to a government, parties have just one more attempt before another election will be automatically called.

Kristersson said he does not want another election, but is “totally prepared” for one and already has a team of people preparing in case.

Ukraine preparing for prisoner of war exchange with Russia, Zelenskyy says

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv is working on a prisoner of war exchange with Russia, “one of the most important agreements reached at the trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi.”

He said Ukraine would submit its proposals to the US, and could “deliver results in the coming weeks.”

“The timeline for implementing this agreement depends on how quickly the Russian side acts and on the American team’s communication with them,” he said.

Acting on the success of the humanitarian operations in Oleshky, Ukraine will also propose 10 other areas in the occupied parts of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions where similar actions are needed, Zelenskyy said.

Kerch Bridge strike shows Ukraine's 'ingenuity and absolute determination to defend itself,' UK's Streeting says

Arriving earlier, UK defence secretary Wes Streeting – who co-chairs the group - said the meeting comes “at a critical time for the war in Ukraine” in what he argued “has been a terrible year for Vladimir Putin.”

“Russian casualties are [at] intolerably high levels as a direct result of his illegal and unnecessary war. The economic costs on his economy and his own people have been catastrophic. And all of those lives and all of those, economic costs are coming with little to no gain. The frontline isn’t moving, and Ukraine continues to show extraordinary resilience, courage and ingenuity.”

Streeting said the meeting was focused on “mobilising the support for allies … to see Ukraine through what will inevitably be a challenging winter.”

“We’re all invested in the, attempt to negotiate a peace, and an end to this conflict that has to be on terms that are acceptable to Ukraine. There can be no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine.”

On the Kerch Bridge strike, he said:

“I think we’ve just seen another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine’s absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression. We stand with Ukraine, as they do that.”

Just like Rutte, he said he expected “a number” of announcements from Ukraine’s allies to help Kyiv in the coming months today.

Ukraine's Kerch bridge strike 'unavoidable' as Ukraine defends itself from aggression, Nato's Rutte says

Over in Brussels, the Ukraine Defence Contact Group is about to meet for their latest talks on Ukraine, including the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge A. Colby.

Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte just arrived and chatted with reporters, telling them he is “relatively optimistic” ahead of the meeting, hoping for “some good announcements this afternoon.”

“A lot of people are working very hard to bring peace to Ukraine. But in the meantime, we have to make sure that they have what they need to get through winter, that they have what they need to be as strong as possible in the peace negotiations.”

On the Kerch Bridge, Rutte said that “it’s important that Ukraine defends itself.”

“And that means also hitting out at logistical nodes; it’s unavoidable that they do that. … We have to see, of course, what exactly happened but at least [from] the media footage, it seems that they were successful.”

Rutte declined to comment on the peace negotiations, saying merely that “the US is playing a crucial part here.”

“I think it’s good that Europe is now at a table – that was one of the outcomes of Abu Dhabi – I think the Europeans have organised themselves now quite well.”

Asked about the renewed Starshield restrictions affecting Ukraine, he said that “relevant parties are working very hard to make sure that as soon as possible, things are back to normal.”

“I know that anyone who can be helpful here is working on this.”

articles.body:
Ethiopia-Eritrea border clashes raise fears of regional war

November 17, 2026

As Ethiopian troops push Tigrayan forces toward the Eritrean border, fears of a new regional war are growing. With tensions rising between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, the Horn of Africa faces uncertain times ahead.

After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.

Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.

According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.

While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.

The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement, in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.

"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.

He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.

The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea

"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.

Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.

Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.

"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.

However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."

Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.

Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads

At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.

Sudan and Egypt, both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD). The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt.

Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts.

Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now.

"The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said.

Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation.

"The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved."

articles.title: How the attack on Crimean Bridge unfolded

articles.body:
How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded

Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.

A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.

How did the seven-stage operation play out?

The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.

But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.

In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.

The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.

Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.

Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".

Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea â the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.

In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

articles.title: Trump to raise Ukraine war in talks with Xi and Putin at APEC
articles.summary: The Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take place between the leaders of China, the US and Russia.
articles.preview: China The southern Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take center stage. President Donald Trump is preparing to sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday in an unprecedented three-way summit of the world's three largest nuclear powers, leaving US allies wondering where they stand.
articles.body:
China

The southern Chinese city of Shenzhen is preparing to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with an unprecedented diplomatic encounter expected to take center stage.

President Donald Trump is preparing to sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday in an unprecedented three-way summit of the world's three largest nuclear powers, leaving US allies wondering where they stand.

The significance of the gathering may have less to do with concrete agreements than with the message it sends about Trump's approach to the world's major powers, said Jonathan Czin, a former CIA China expert now at the Brookings Institution.

"What will be more important than the substance of this meeting is going to be the subtext," Czin said. He said US allies in Asia and Europe could see the Trump administration as more focused on accommodating China and Russia than countering their influence.

The meeting marks a striking departure from the strategy of Trump's first administration, when Washington identified China and Russia as its principal geopolitical competitors.

"We've gone 180 degrees from saying these are the main problems we face in the national security space for the US government, to now we're going to have a major meeting with these two leaders," Czin said.

The summit is expected to focus on nuclear arms control, with Trump also seeking to discuss the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine. Trump said Monday he intended to raise Ukraine with Xi and Putin, despite administration officials saying last week that the war would not be part of the discussions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern about the prospect of major powers discussing global spheres of influence without Ukraine at the table.

Putin may emerge as the biggest beneficiary of the gathering, Czin said, gaining an opportunity to share the international stage with Trump and Xi despite Russia's isolation from much of the West.

"I think it's a political coup for Putin," Czin said. "Of the three men involved in this meeting, I think he probably is the one who's gaining the most."

Xi also has incentives to participate, Czin said, as the gathering allows Beijing to demonstrate its central role in international affairs while seeking relief from US pressure.

Trump has said he wants to pursue a new nuclear arms agreement that would include China. But Beijing has repeatedly resisted US efforts to engage on nuclear weapons, even as it expands its arsenal.

Czin expects little substantive progress, describing the likely outcome as a superficial exchange rather than the beginning of meaningful arms control negotiations.

The summit comes as Trump seeks to reassert his standing on the world stage following Republican losses in the midterm elections. Czin said the president may see direct engagement with Xi and Putin as an opportunity to demonstrate his influence and build his legacy.

But Trump will also need to show he has not made concessions that undermine US interests, Czin said.

The president must send a clear signal about American priorities and intentions, he said, while reassuring allies that their interests have not been set aside.

For Wang Huiyao, founder and president of the Center for China and Globalization, the gathering represents an opportunity for the three major powers to help shape a new international consensus.

“Last time when China, US and Russian leaders get together, that was 80 some years ago,” he said.

“Now we are at another turning point, we are at a more fragmented world, we are getting to a multipolar world, and the world is lacking strong directions.”

Ukraine war

One area where that could have an immediate impact is the conflict in Ukraine.

Breakthrough is unlikely, yet the three leaders may work out something on which progress can be made at the platforms such as United Nations and G20, said Wang.

"This three leaders' meeting could, you know, kick off some peace consensus that they can really get further strengthened at the UN with the Security Council, other members and even with the European Union and Ukraine to have a peace summit maybe at the UN sometime,” Wang said.

“Then maybe at G20 next month, there could be some even more progress on the ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine," he added.

For Wang Yiwei, Director of the Institute of International Affairs at Renmin University of China, the trialateral summit will only be a complementary effort if the three leaders discussed the Ukraine conflict.

“Ukraine and Russia, these two parts, need to directly negotiate,” he said. “But they're not trusting each other.”

The endorsement from China and US are essential for both sides in the negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, said Wang Yiwei.

The meeting would also underscore China's growing ambitions to play a more active role in international affairs, said Wang Huiyao.

“I think we are coming to a stage that China is the second largest economy, one of the, or probably the second largest military power and even if China is not there, it could also provide guarantor roles, could provide all those active roles there, and all the countries are coming to China and looking for help,” he said.

For Washington, the summit also comes at a politically important moment.

President Trump faces pressure to demonstrate that his foreign and economic policies can deliver results at home, while managing relations with both Beijing and Moscow.

“For President Trump also it is very important because after the ‘Waterloo’ in the midterm election,” said Wang Yiwei.

“So they need to get some beef back and then to show the policy still succeeds," he added.

articles.title: Trump meets regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.summary: Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.
articles.preview: Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative. MANILA: United States President Donald Trump met the leaders of regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, at the start of an Asian trip that also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.
articles.body:
Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.

MANILA: United States President Donald Trump met the leaders of regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, at the start of an Asian trip that also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.

Trump arrived in the Philippine capital at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, and began his three-day regional visit with the first meeting in two years of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific democracies.

"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump said.

Trump's three-day trip to Asia, which also includes the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, comes after his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections, plus spy allegations and new US curbs on China's access to AI chips that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce.

ECONOMIC TENSIONS AHEAD OF XI MEETING

It was Trump's first meeting of the Quad grouping – which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who will host Trump and others at a meeting this week of the 21-member Pacific Rim grouping APEC, has previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

In a statement after the leaders' meeting, the Quad expressed "grave concerns" about "economic coercion", including through arbitrary export restrictions.

While the statement did not name any country, the US and Japan have complained about China’s restrictions on exports of rare earths vital to the manufacturing of everything from electric cars to cell phones.

China has effectively shut off exports of key critical minerals to Japan for nearly a year as relations between Asia’s two largest economies have nosedived.

Underlining tensions ahead of Trump's meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, when they are expected to discuss a fragile trade-war truce that will expire in January, China's foreign ministry also had earlier accused the US of "economic coercion" over its latest restrictions on Chinese access to advanced chips.

JOINT EXERCISES AND AI

The Quad statement flagged plans for joint military exercises next year featuring maritime patrol aircraft, and reaffirmed a commitment to an accelerator scheme to coordinate and fund the development of artificial intelligence.

"We want to ensure that the future of this critical technology is dominated by nations that share our values and our common interests and make sure that it turns out to be as good as it can be," Trump said, referring to the AI plans.

Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell credited Washington's top diplomat, Marco Rubio, with the timing and reconvening of the Quad, which he said had lost ambition under Trump.

"Part of what he (Rubio) is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you're going to go into a trilateral meeting," said Campbell, co-founder of The Asia Group, referring to Thursday's US-China-Russia talks.

"Today’s meeting has given fresh momentum to our shared vision for a free, open, peaceful and prosperous Indo-Pacific, with concrete goals for the next phase of our cooperation," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said in a post on X.

PROTESTS IN MANILA

Trump arrived in the Philippines at the end of a summit there of another regional body, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. After the Quad meeting, he joined a US-ASEAN "Special Summit".

He will meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on Wednesday, before heading to Shenzhen.

Demonstrators had gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and the scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.

At the ASEAN summit on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed what he called the "truly extraordinary" economic achievements of China and ASEAN in the face of global trade restrictions, expressing Beijing's commitment to free trade and the need to "stand united, ward off interference, and work together".

China is ASEAN's largest trading partner and a key source of investment, but the biggest economies of the bloc - which has a combined GDP of more than US$3.9 trillion - want to deepen ties with the US despite protracted trade and diplomatic uncertainty under the Trump administration.

ASEAN's leaders held meetings on Tuesday involving counterparts from Japan, South Korea, China and India.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to work with ASEAN to boost regional economic and energy resilience and to strengthen supply chains, including on critical minerals.

"While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play an ever more proactive role," Takaichi said.

Trump also signed a joint statement on trade with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. He said Thailand would eliminate all tariffs on US exports and remove substantial non-tariff barriers under a trade agreement expected to be finalised in the coming weeks.

The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24 per cent of its total shipments this year.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.
articles.preview: Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people. Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.

BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.

Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.

Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.

Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.

Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.

His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

articles.title: L’Estonia ha un piano digitale per difendersi dalla Russia
articles.summary: Tallinn sta trasferendo i servizi della pubblica amministrazione sul cloud per mantenere operativo il governo, anche dall’estero, in caso di attacchi informatici o militari
articles.preview: Immaginate il generale francese Charles de Gaulle, in esilio a Londra durante la seconda guerra mondiale, impegnato a dirigere il governo della Francia libera accedendo al cloud. I funzionari estoni si stanno preparando per uno scenario simile con una strategia per rafforzare la capacità di resistere a situazioni catastrofiche (hukukindlus in estone) che permetterà di gestire dall’estero i servizi digitali del governo nel caso di un’occupazione straniera.
articles.body:
Immaginate il generale francese Charles de Gaulle, in esilio a Londra durante la seconda guerra mondiale, impegnato a dirigere il governo della Francia libera accedendo al cloud.

I funzionari estoni si stanno preparando per uno scenario simile con una strategia per rafforzare la capacità di resistere a situazioni catastrofiche (hukukindlus in estone) che permetterà di gestire dall’estero i servizi digitali del governo nel caso di un’occupazione straniera.

Il paese baltico, che ha 1,3 milioni di abitanti e condivide un confine di 294 chilometri con la Russia, teme di diventare uno degli obiettivi principali di Mosca se questa decidesse d’invadere uno stato dell’Unione europea. I servizi di sicurezza hanno più volte avvertito che la Russia sta conducendo una guerra ibrida contro l’Europa, e l’Estonia ha accusato Mosca di attacchi informatici, incendi dolosi e danni ai cavi sottomarini per la trasmissione dei dati.

Ora Tallinn si prepara a trasferire i suoi servizi pubblici sul cloud “nel caso che i data center fossero distrutti o se ci fosse un’occupazione militare che impedisse di operare”, spiega Tõnu Grünberg, uno degli artefici della nuova strategia ed ex vicesegretario generale per le infrastrutture digitali e la cibersicurezza del ministero estone della giustizia e degli affari digitali.

L’Estonia ha già un backup dei dati nella sua “ambasciata digitale” in Lussemburgo, di fatto una copia di tutti i suoi documenti ufficiali, dai registri anagrafici a quelli catastali fino ai codici delle leggi.

“Ora vogliamo andare davvero online, qualunque cosa accada”, afferma Grünberg. “Tutti i servizi fondamentali dovranno rimanere pienamente operativi”.

Il governo estone sta sviluppando applicazioni sicure su piattaforme cloud come Microsoft Azure e Amazon Web Services, oltre che su una piattaforma statale. Il trasferimento del sistema alla sua ambasciata digitale e ad altre sedi in Europa è in corso, sottolinea Grünberg, che pochi giorni fa ha assunto l’incarico di amministratore delegato della Levira, un’azienda estone d’infrastrutture tecnologiche.

Allan Allmere, consulente per le infrastrutture tecnologiche al ministero della giustizia e degli affari digitali, ha dichiarato a Politico che l’Estonia vuole ridurre al minimo le conseguenze negative anche nello scenario peggiore.

“Idealmente vorremmo realizzare sistemi capaci di resistere a qualunque crisi, ma sappiamo bene che è impossibile prevedere o eliminare del tutto i rischi”, dichiara. “Anche nelle situazioni peggiori, però, dobbiamo avere una base solida per ricostruire lo stato digitale estone”.

Il precedente del 2007

Gli estoni sanno bene che rischi corrono i servizi digitali fin dal 2007, quando per ventidue giorni il paese affrontò un’ondata di attacchi informatici che mise fuori uso buona parte dei servizi privati e della pubblica amministrazione. Le autorità attribuirono gli attacchi alla Russia.

L’episodio, considerato il primo caso di attacco informatico su vasta scala contro uno stato, spinse l’Estonia a riorganizzare completamente le sue infrastrutture digitali, trasformandola in uno dei paesi più digitalizzati del mondo.

“Ha adottato una linea straordinariamente lungimirante in termini di digitalizzazione dei servizi della pubblica amministrazione”, afferma Joseph Jarnecki, ricercatore senior del centro studi Royal united services institute (Rusi) di Londra.

Secondo Allmere, la pianificazione per le situazioni critiche punta a garantire che “non si debba mai ricominciare da zero”.

Gli attacchi recenti ai data center in Russia hanno evidenziato fino a che punto i servizi digitali siano diventati cruciali per i paesi in guerra. Il mese scorso l’Ucraina ha colpito tre data center del provider russo Yandex, dimostrando che gli attacchi di questo tipo hanno ormai un’efficacia paragonabile a quelli contro le centrali da cui dipendono l’elettricità, il riscaldamento e il carburante di militari e civili.

Il piano nazionale estone per la resilienza alle catastrofi è un esempio significativo di come molti paesi stiano cercando di proteggere i propri cittadini e i propri servizi attraverso la delocalizzazione. Fino a poco tempo fa si pensava che fosse più sicuro mantenere il controllo dei servizi digitali all’interno del territorio, archiviando i dati localmente e costruendo tecnologie e data center dentro i confini del paese.

Oggi però gli stati – soprattutto quelli più esposti ai rischi di un conflitto – stanno ripensando questo approccio, in modo da diluire i rischi per le infrastrutture digitali.

Il 12 novembre il Regno Unito e la Norvegia hanno annunciato la possibile creazione di ambasciate digitali nei due paesi per custodire in sicurezza i rispettivi dati.

Anche l’Estonia sta studiando “alleanze con paesi terzi considerati affidabili” per rafforzare la sua sicurezza digitale, “perché non è vero che siamo più forti quando abbiamo tutto all’interno del territorio nazionale”, dice Jarnecki.

L’interruzione dei servizi Microsoft che il 12 novembre ha colpito aziende e governi in tutto il mondo ha evidenziato la necessità per gli stati di diversificare i loro fornitori di servizi cloud e digitali per evitare conseguenze troppo pesanti in caso di attacchi informatici o problemi tecnici.

Secondo Allmere, il governo estone è pronto ad affrontare nuove sfide. “La prima era assicurarsi che i dati dello stato non andassero persi”, dice riferendosi all’ambasciata digitale in Lussemburgo che fa da backup. “La prossima sarà garantire che lo stato continui a funzionare, grazie a quegli stessi dati, nell’eventualità di una crisi”.

Ma non basta. “Dobbiamo essere sicuri che i dati rimangano leggibili e utilizzabili anche tra decenni”, conclude Allmere. ◆

articles.title: Algeria threatens to target drug traffickers at 'source' amid Morocco tensions
articles.summary: Algeria is declaring war on drugs. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune is threatening tougher action, warning that the fight must target the source of the problem.
articles.preview: news Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Sunday threatened to take action against drugs at "the source" amid longstanding accusations by Algiers that neighbouring Morocco was behind drug trafficking into the country. Tebboune did not name Morocco in an address at the Algerian Supreme Court, but Algiers has often blamed Morocco as being the source of drugs trafficked through their shared border.
